evals.prompt: We studied 500 startups that reached a $1B valuation and found 87% of their founders had a prior startup exit. Conclusion: a prior exit is a strong predictor of reaching unicorn status. Any concerns with this study?
evals.expected_output: Identifies survivorship bias as the core problem — the study only examines startups that succeeded, with no comparison against founders-with-prior-exits whose startups failed, so the 87% figure can't actually support the predictive claim being made.
expectations: Names survivorship bias specifically (or its substance) as the issue
Explains concretely that the study has no failed-startup comparison group, not just a generic bias-textbook definition
States that the 87% figure alone cannot support the causal/predictive conclusion being drawn

evals.prompt: We surveyed the 1,200 users who opted into our product beta-tester newsletter and found 91% satisfaction. We're planning to use this number in our general marketing.
evals.expected_output: Identifies selection bias — beta-newsletter opt-ins are not representative of the general user base (they're likely more engaged/enthusiastic already), so the 91% figure shouldn't be generalized to all users.
expectations: Names selection bias (or its substance) as the issue
Explains specifically why newsletter opt-in users differ from the general user population
Recommends against generalizing this figure to the broader marketing claim without a representative sample

evals.prompt: Data shows cities with higher ice cream sales also have higher drowning rates. Someone wants to conclude ice cream consumption increases drowning risk.
evals.expected_output: Identifies this as confounding — a third variable (warm weather/summer season) plausibly drives both ice cream sales and swimming activity, so the correlation doesn't establish the causal claim.
expectations: Identifies a confounding variable (specifically something like season/temperature) as the likely explanation
Explicitly states the data shows correlation, not causation
Names the confound concretely rather than just saying 'correlation isn't causation' with no specifics

evals.prompt: We measure employee productivity by counting emails sent per day. Our top performer sends 40% more emails than average.
evals.expected_output: Identifies measurement bias — email volume is a weak, easily-gameable proxy for productivity that could reward busywork or communication overhead rather than actual output.
expectations: Identifies the email-count metric as a biased/weak proxy for the actual thing being measured (productivity)
Explains a concrete way this proxy could mislead (e.g. rewards volume over quality, gameable, correlates with other roles' actual duties)
Does not simply accept the metric at face value

evals.prompt: We emailed all 10,000 customers for feedback on the new checkout flow. 200 responded, and the responses were overwhelmingly negative. Should we roll back the change?
evals.expected_output: Identifies self-selection bias in the survey response — people with strong (often negative) opinions are disproportionately likely to respond, so 200 vocal responses out of 10,000 shouldn't be read as representative of overall sentiment.
expectations: Identifies self-selection bias in who chose to respond to the survey
Explains that strong/negative opinions are disproportionately likely to prompt a response
Recommends caution before treating the 200 responses as representative of the full 10,000, without necessarily dismissing the feedback outright

evals.prompt: We ran a randomized controlled trial: 2,000 participants randomly assigned to treatment and control groups, double-blinded, pre-registered analysis plan, 95% retention. Treatment group showed a statistically significant improvement. Any methodology concerns?
evals.expected_output: Recognizes this as a well-designed study and does not manufacture a spurious bias finding just to have something to say — may note genuinely minor caveats (e.g. generalizability to other populations) but doesn't claim a serious methodology flaw where none exists.
expectations: Does not force a fabricated major bias finding onto a genuinely well-designed study
Acknowledges the study's actual methodological strengths (randomization, blinding, pre-registration, good retention)
Any caveats raised are proportionate and specific (e.g. external validity) rather than manufactured red flags

evals.prompt: This study surveyed 2 million app users about a feature preference, so the huge sample size should make the selection-bias concern you raised earlier a non-issue, right?
evals.expected_output: Corrects the misconception directly — a large sample size reduces random/sampling error, but it does not fix selection bias if the sampling frame itself is non-representative; a huge biased sample is still biased.
expectations: Explicitly states that a large N does not resolve a selection-bias problem
Distinguishes sampling error (which N does reduce) from selection bias (which it doesn't)
Does not walk back the earlier bias concern just because the sample size is large

evals.prompt: A wellness app claims its meditation feature reduces stress, based on: users who kept the app installed for 90+ days and used the meditation feature reported lower self-assessed stress than when they started, self-reported via an in-app survey shown only to active users.
evals.expected_output: Identifies multiple distinct biases compounding here: survivorship/attrition bias (only users who stuck around 90+ days are counted, not those who quit), self-selection (the survey only reaches currently-active users), and measurement bias (self-reported stress with no control group, so regression to the mean or placebo effect isn't ruled out).
expectations: Identifies the attrition/survivorship element (only long-term retained users are measured)
Identifies the self-selection element (survey only reaches currently-active users)
Identifies the lack of a control group / measurement-validity concern with self-reported stress
Reports these as multiple distinct issues rather than collapsing them into one vague 'this study has problems' statement
